question: An unexpected message urgently asks you to verify your password. What is the safest response?
options: Use the message link immediately
Reply with your password
Verify through an official trusted channel and report the message
Forward the request to coworkers
explanation: Urgency and credential requests are warning signs. Use a known route and report the message; do not use the supplied link.

question: A familiar display name appears, but the sender address looks unusual. What should you do?
options: Trust the display name
Inspect the full sender and independently verify the request
Open any attachment to identify the sender
Send a test password
explanation: Display names can be misleading. Verify the full sender and context through a separate trusted channel.

question: You receive an unexpected QR code asking you to sign in. What is a safer action?
options: Scan it immediately
Share it publicly
Use the official app or known site instead and report the message
Enter credentials to preview the page
explanation: A QR code hides its destination. Use a known route rather than scanning an unsolicited code.

question: Why should important accounts use unique passwords?
options: It makes them easier to remember
It limits the impact if one service exposes a password
It removes the need for updates
It proves the site is genuine
explanation: Unique passwords prevent one exposed credential from being reused against other accounts.

question: What is a safe way to manage many unique passwords?
options: Reuse one memorable password
Store them in an approved password manager
Send them to yourself in chat
Write them on a public note
explanation: An approved password manager can generate and protect unique credentials without unsafe reuse.

question: A colleague asks you to send your password so they can finish a task. What should you do?
options: Send it once
Share it in a private chat
Do not share it; use approved delegated access or contact support
Change it to a simple temporary value
explanation: Passwords and one-time codes should not be shared. Use an approved access-sharing process.

question: An MFA approval prompt appears when you are not signing in. What should you do?
options: Approve it to stop notifications
Deny it and report the unexpected prompt
Send the code to the requester
Ignore all future MFA prompts
explanation: Unexpected MFA prompts can indicate an attempted sign-in. Deny and report them.

question: Which statement about MFA is most accurate?
options: MFA makes every attack impossible
MFA adds a second verification layer beyond a password
MFA means passwords no longer need protection
MFA codes are safe to share with support
explanation: MFA adds a layer of protection, but users still need to protect credentials and approve only sign-ins they initiated.

question: When available, which sign-in approach is designed to resist many fake-site credential attacks?
options: A passkey or security key
A password sent by email
A code read to an unknown caller
A shared team password
explanation: Passkeys and security keys can provide phishing-resistant authentication when correctly supported and enrolled.

question: A caller claiming to be an executive urgently requests a confidential file and says not to tell anyone. What is safest?
options: Send it to be helpful
Verify independently using the normal process
Ask for their password
Ignore approval policy because it is urgent
explanation: Urgency, secrecy, and authority are common pressure tactics. Verify through a separate trusted channel.

question: A vendor requests a payment-account change by email. What should you do?
options: Update it from the email alone
Verify using a known contact and required approval workflow
Reply asking them to repeat the account number
Share the request on social media
explanation: Payment changes should be independently verified and follow normal approval controls.

question: A message asks you to bypass a normal approval step because it is confidential. What is a good response?
options: Follow the standard process and verify the request
Make an exception without records
Share your MFA code
Delete the policy
explanation: Confidentiality and urgency should not override established approvals. Verify and report unusual pressure.

question: A link in an unsolicited message leads to a sign-in page with a slightly misspelled domain. What should you do?
options: Enter your password to test it
Use a bookmark or official app and report the message
Forward the link to friends
Disable browser warnings
explanation: Look-alike domains can be deceptive. Use a known route; the project never visits submitted indicators.

question: Your browser shows a security warning on a site needed for work. What is the safest next step?
options: Bypass it without review
Stop and contact IT or use an approved alternative
Install a browser add-on from the warning
Enter credentials in a new tab
explanation: Do not bypass unexplained warnings; use approved support channels.

question: A pop-up says your browser is out of date and offers a download. What should you do?
options: Download it immediately
Close the pop-up and update through the official browser mechanism
Share the download with coworkers
Disable updates
explanation: Install updates through a trusted, official update channel, not an unsolicited pop-up.

question: You see unusual file changes and a security warning on a work device. What is the best first step?
options: Continue working and delete the warning
Contact the incident-response or IT channel promptly and follow instructions
Try random cleanup utilities
Copy work files to personal storage
explanation: Prompt reporting lets trained responders coordinate safe handling. Avoid improvised cleanup or copying data.

question: Which practice supports recovery from disruptive incidents?
options: Tested, protected backups
One shared administrator account
Turning off updates
Keeping the only copy on one device
explanation: Protected, tested backups are a key resilience measure, alongside patching, least privilege, monitoring, and response preparation.

question: Why is least privilege useful for limiting impact?
options: It gives everyone permanent administrator access
It limits access to what a role needs
It disables incident reporting
It makes backups unnecessary
explanation: Limiting privileges can reduce how much an account or process can affect.

question: A form requests personal information unrelated to its stated purpose. What should you do?
options: Provide extra details to be safe
Pause and verify the request and approved data-collection process
Post the data in a group chat
Use a coworker's information
explanation: Data minimization means sharing only what is needed through approved channels.

question: Before sharing a document externally, what should you check?
options: Recipient, permissions, and whether the data is approved for sharing
Only the file name
Whether the document has a colorful theme
Nothing if the link works
explanation: Verify the recipient and access scope, and follow data-handling policy.

question: You accidentally send a sensitive file to the wrong recipient. What is appropriate?
options: Wait and hope nobody notices
Report promptly through privacy/security procedures and follow guidance
Forward it to more people
Delete the sent email and assume it is recalled
explanation: Prompt reporting enables the organization to assess and coordinate the response. Do not assume deletion or recall solved it.

question: At a public location, two wireless networks have similar names. What should you do?
options: Choose randomly
Confirm the official network name through staff or a trusted source
Use both at once
Enter work credentials in a pop-up
explanation: Network names can be imitated. Confirm the correct network and use approved secure access.

question: A public Wi-Fi sign-in page asks you to install an unknown profile. What is safest?
options: Install it to save time
Stop and ask the service provider or IT through a trusted route
Share it with coworkers
Disable device protections
explanation: Unknown profiles can change device settings. Do not install them without trusted verification.

question: What is a sensible practice on a shared public network?
options: Enable file sharing for everyone
Disable unnecessary sharing and use approved secure access
Reuse a password on every service
Ignore device update prompts forever
explanation: Reduce unnecessary exposure and use the organization-approved access method.

question: Your work phone is missing. What should you do?
options: Wait a few days
Contact the service desk/security team promptly and follow approved device steps
Post all account details online
Borrow an unknown person's phone and log in
explanation: Fast reporting gives authorized teams a chance to apply approved account/device protections.

question: A flashlight app asks for access to contacts and messages. What is a good response?
options: Grant every permission
Review whether access is necessary and avoid or remove untrusted apps
Share your phone PIN with the app publisher
Turn off all device updates
explanation: Review permissions and install apps only from trusted, approved sources.

question: Which combination improves basic mobile protection?
options: No screen lock and delayed updates
Strong screen lock, current updates, and trusted apps
Shared PIN and open sharing
Unknown profiles and disabled alerts
explanation: A screen lock, updates, and trusted app sources are core defensive practices.

question: You clicked an unexpected link but did not notice anything unusual. What should you do?
options: Hide it to avoid trouble
Report promptly and state exactly what happened
Delete all records
Tell only friends
explanation: Reporting is useful even when you are unsure. Share facts, not assumptions, and follow response guidance.

question: What details are useful when reporting a suspicious event?
options: Approximate time, device, what you observed, and actions taken
A guess about who is responsible
Passwords and authentication codes
Only a screenshot posted publicly
explanation: Clear observations help responders triage. Never include passwords or one-time codes.

question: After reporting an incident, what should you do?
options: Follow the response team's guidance and avoid ad-hoc investigation
Probe the suspected system yourself
Contact suspected external infrastructure
Delete evidence without direction
explanation: Authorized responders coordinate next steps. Do not scan, contact, or investigate external indicators yourself.
